# Summary of Political Manifesto

This manifesto presents a vision for national governance focused on several key policy areas, emphasising action over rhetoric and accountability in government.

## Economic Policy

The document advocates for fiscal responsibility, arguing that government spending has become excessive and unsustainable. It proposes £12 billion in annual savings through reducing civil service posts and cutting public bodies. Of these savings, £8 billion would reduce borrowing while £4 billion would fund tax cuts. The manifesto commits to maintaining central bank independence for interest rate decisions and opposes adopting a common European currency.

Pensioner support features prominently, including proposals to halve council tax for over-65s, increase state pensions in line with earnings rather than prices, and create new savings accounts with government contributions.

## Education

The manifesto emphasises school discipline as fundamental to effective learning. It proposes giving head teachers full control over admissions and expulsions, with disruptive pupils directed to specialist schools. Teachers would receive protection from malicious allegations and reduced paperwork.

Funding would follow pupils, allowing parental choice to drive resources. The document proposes 600,000 additional school places, vocational grants for teenagers, and scrapping university tuition fees. It advocates for rigorous examination standards and curriculum reform.

## Healthcare

Healthcare spending would increase to £2,000 per head annually. The manifesto proposes abolishing centrally-set targets, reducing administrative bodies, and giving hospitals freedom over staffing and investment. Patients and GPs would choose care providers, with funding following patient choices. Infection control receives particular attention, with proposals to reinstate ward matrons with authority to close wards for cleaning.

## Crime and Security

The document proposes recruiting 5,000 additional police officers annually, establishing elected local police commissioners, and implementing zero-tolerance neighbourhood policing. Prison capacity would expand by 20,000 places, with sentences served in full. Drug treatment programmes would expand significantly, including 25,000 residential rehabilitation places.

## Immigration

The manifesto proposes establishing a unified border control force, implementing 24-hour port surveillance, and introducing an Australian-style points system for work permits. It advocates withdrawing from certain international agreements to establish national control over asylum policy, processing applications outside the country, and setting annual immigration limits determined by parliament.

## Governance and Constitutional Matters

Proposals include abolishing regional assemblies, returning powers to local authorities, reducing parliamentary seats by 20 per cent, and ensuring that legislation affecting only one constituent nation is decided by representatives from that nation alone. The manifesto commits to reforming the upper legislative chamber through increased elected membership.

## Foreign Policy and Defence

Defence spending would increase by £2.7 billion for front-line forces. The document opposes a proposed European constitutional treaty, promising a referendum within six months, and commits to negotiating return of certain regulatory powers from European institutions. International development spending would increase toward 0.7 per cent of national income by 2013.

## Environment and Transport

Environmental proposals include phasing out harmful chemicals, incentivising low-emission vehicles, protecting green belt land, and promoting brownfield development. Transport policy includes modernising road networks, reviewing speed cameras, and extending rail franchises to encourage private investment.

The manifesto concludes by presenting specific actions for implementation within the first day and month of taking office, emphasising immediate accountability for stated commitments.

# Summary of 2005 General Election Manifesto

## Core Principles

The manifesto is built on three principles: individual freedom with minimal unnecessary government interference, fairness through provision of essential services (education, healthcare, pensions, environment, policing), and trust through democratic accountability and decentralisation of power.

## Healthcare Proposals

Key commitments include free personal care for elderly and disabled people, quicker diagnostic pathways using both public and private facilities, free eye and dental check-ups, expanded prescription charge exemptions, recruitment of additional medical staff, and removal of centralised bureaucratic targets. Prevention initiatives include banning smoking in enclosed public places, school meal nutrition standards, and restricting unhealthy food advertising to children.

## Education and Skills

The manifesto proposes abolishing university tuition fees, cutting infant class sizes to an average of 20 pupils, ensuring core subjects are taught by qualified specialists, and reducing external testing. Other commitments include expanding Children's Centres, reforming school discipline policies, combining academic and vocational qualifications into a diploma system, and maintaining free school transport.

## Economic Approach

Proposals include adhering to fiscal rules limiting government borrowing and debt, giving independent auditing powers to scrutinise budget figures, simplifying business taxation, introducing a 50% tax rate on income above £100,000 annually, abolishing Council Tax in favour of income-based local taxation, cutting stamp duty thresholds, and reducing regulations on businesses.

## Pensions and Benefits

Commitments include guaranteeing increased basic pension from age 75 linked to earnings, introducing a residency-based citizen's pension addressing women's pension inequality, increasing maternity pay, reforming employment support programmes, abolishing the Child Support Agency, providing winter fuel payments to severely disabled people, and improving compensation for workers affected by failed company pension schemes.

## Crime and Justice

Proposals include recruiting 10,000 additional police officers, expanding community support officers, implementing community justice panels for non-violent offenders, using Acceptable Behaviour Contracts, improving prison education and skills training, creating a UK Border Force, opposing identity card schemes, opposing reductions in jury trial rights, and reforming asylum assessment processes.

## Local Communities

Key policies include replacing Council Tax with income-based local taxation, releasing public land for 100,000 affordable homes, freeing councils from central government controls, merging inspection bodies, protecting post office networks, and setting municipal waste reduction targets including 60% household recycling within seven years.

## International Affairs

The manifesto criticises military intervention in Iraq as lacking proper legal authority, commits to working within international institutions, supports UN reform and EU constitutional changes subject to referendum, advocates increasing international aid to 0.7% of national income, and proposes working for fair trade agreements whilst ending agricultural subsidies that harm developing economies.

## Environment

Environmental policies throughout the manifesto include achieving renewable energy targets of 20% by 2020, introducing carbon taxation, not replacing nuclear power stations, implementing vehicle taxation based on emissions, promoting public transport investment, establishing environmental tribunals, and pressing for international climate agreements based on per-capita emissions convergence.

## Governance Reform

Constitutional proposals include curbing prime ministerial powers, requiring parliamentary approval for military action, establishing a predominantly elected second chamber, introducing proportional representation for elections, reducing ministerial numbers, strengthening parliamentary scrutiny, and enhancing devolution to Scotland and Wales.
